reviews.text: The battles are potent. The rest: in the story, Pvt Ryan's life matters more than others because of a PR opportunity for Uncle Sam, as a single death is a tragedy, as Stalin apparently didn't say but America loves to think. This obvious point is almost confronted when the soldiers question their mission, but brushed off with swelling music. When leaders sacrifice people for only sentiment in return, Spielberg sees a heroic call to duty where Vonnegut (who saw the war) saw cold senseless tragedy.

Pure propagande pro-USA. La scène d’ouverture est incroyablement bien filmée, rien à dire là-dessus. Mais faire passer les Américains pour les héros et quasiment tous les autres comme des monstres, ça ne passe pas pour moi. Le film est vraiment très manichéen dans sa manière de présenter les camps : les soldats américains sont humanisés, courageux et prêts à se sacrifier, tandis que les Allemands sont beaucoup plus souvent réduits au rôle d’ennemis cruels et sans véritable "profondeur". Et soyons honnêtes : sacrifier autant d’hommes juste pour retrouver Ryan… mdrr. Comme si les États-Unis allaient faire preuve d’une telle « empathie » envers chq famille dont plusieurs fils seraient morts à la guerre. Des mères ont forcément perdu plusieurs enfants pendant le conflit, et ça a dû arriver des milliers de fois. Ce n’est pas comme si les mères de l’époque n’avaient qu’un seul fils. Donc quoi ? On aurait dû envoyer une mission spéciale pour chq famille ayant perdu plusieurs enfants ? 😭 Je trouve que le film utilise cette histoire pour construire un récit très héroïque et patriotique autour de l’armée américaine. Et même si ça fonctionne ( un peu)  émotionnellement, j’ai du mal (énormément) avec le message derrière. Après, techniquement, le film est vraiment impressionnant, surtout son ouverture. Mais sur le fond, beaucoup moins convaincant. Juste arrêtons les films pro-USA et surtout pro-Israël

Now here's a film I hadn't seen in over two decades. I never cared much for this one, in part because I'm not the biggest fan of war cinema, and in part because I think Spielberg is a director who should stay away from anything too serious. And sure enough, there's too much misplaced sentiment here to make it a good film. The casting isn't great either, the music is icky, and the film is way too long, with too many lulls dragging the whole thing down. But I did find a bit more to enjoy here compared to the first time I watched it, mostly in the action scenes. But then you have films like 1917, and there's no more need for Spielberg's tomfoolery. A massively overrated war flick.

Damn, what a shell of a movie. Hollow through and through. This movie made me feel absolutely nothing, not gonna lie. I mean, pew pew, explosion, pew pew... cool gunfight scenes...I guess? The opening scene is shot well, to be fair. But still, I don't watch movies for specific scenes. What kind of fast-food trash bastardization is that? If a movie is good, its entirety can stand on its own two legs; this one just crawls like a paraplegic who was shoved off their wheelchair. I mean, at least to me, even the acting felt subpar at times. If I can think of one good thing about this movie, I'd say the sound design was an "good"...that's honestly about it. I don't really understand the critical acclaim this movie gets. I won't even get started on the propaganda machine this movie fed into. I mean, I get it; at its core it's an "America, fuck yeah!" movie, but any semblance of nuance it tried to push felt forced. I'm not oblivious to the fact it tried to squeeze in the "war is hell, war never changes" shtick with a dab of the "look at all the guys you were introduced to throughout the movie die one by one to save this one guy so that the higher-ups can get their successful PR stunt" narrative, but, fuck me, was it poorly done. Also, although this might be more indicative of my desensitization, the "violence" in this movie didn't feel like it was anything out of the ordinary for a war movie. Also, what a stinker from Spielberg; coming from just watching Schindler's List to this, is it the same Spielberg? The fuck? I get it though; they are fundamentally different movies, but GOD DAMN, man. Left me wanting my 3 hours back.

“Tell me I’ve lived a good life. Tell me I’m a good man” Someone else said Saving Private Ryan works for a metaphor as US involvement in wars in general, in the sense that there’s always a private Ryan to save, a cause to fight for, and the sacrifice made will always be greater than the life saved. In trying to convince the audience that this great sacrifice is the point of war or why it’s necessary, the film misses the fact that this is precisely why war is irredeemably pointless. The film wants to portray all our lead heroes as victims of brutality who want it to end, but also encourages them to be perpetrators of brutality. Upham is the best example of this. He starts the film as a staunch pacifist, someone who wants to bring an end to the brutality on both sides through strict adherence to the Geneva conventions. By the end of the film however, motivated by revenge, he gives into his rage and kills a surrendered German soldier, starting the cycle of violence and brutality once again. The film frames this loss of empathy as heroic. None of my issues with the film are in the directing/filmmaking of it. Spielberg is great and he’s really firing off all cylinders here. But none of that matters (in fact it might make it worse) if the script that directing is supporting creates a world where war is always justified as long as you have a private to save.

I just watched this movie for the first time in 30 years. And while the film is nothing short of an astounding technical achievement, it is as morally and philosophically bankrupt as a film like this could possibly be. ﻿ ﻿Setting aside the events that led up to D-Day and the US entry into a two-front war, this film makes two arguments that I find absolutely appalling: ﻿ ﻿1) That a pacifist subjected to the horrors of war can be thus justified in the committing of a cold-blooded murder. ﻿2) That all who come after owe it to those who gave their lives to be better people because of their sacrifice. ﻿ ﻿When the Captain says "Earn this" to Ryan, I thought that was a really lousy thing to do to another human being. The plot had already established that not only had Ryan had no say in the mission, he vehemently disagreed with it, and wanted nothing to do with it. So for the captain to say that is to put a burden on Ryan that he in no way deserved. ﻿ ﻿But that isn't even the point of that line. Spielberg is trying to tell all of us that we owe it to those who died to earn their sacrifice. And while one can certainly commend them for ending the tyranny of the Nazis, that doesn't mean we all owe it to them to live the lives that they did not get to. Their sacrifice was in the name of freedom. To me, this film seems to make the argument that the sacrifice was in the name of war. ﻿ ﻿Captain Miller could have died anywhere in Europe. He and his team could have died on Omaha Beach. But because they died on that bridge, that doesn't make Private Ryan indebted to them for a sacrifice he did not ask for. And to see a broken old man on that beach 50 years later asking his wife for validation is just piling on. ﻿ ﻿And Upham's murder of the German soldier he previously campaigned to release is somehow meant to show that the horrors of war can change even the least warlike of men. But the manner in which this happens is in purely cold blood, as justification for Upham watching him shoot the captain. Upham has a perfect position to fire his weapon in combat, and the movie could have done that. Instead, Upham takes the prisoners, and shoots the one in cold blood. ﻿ ﻿Nothing justifies this murder. We are meant to see Upham reshaped by war, but to what end? That murder is justified in some context? Upham's lack of remorse in his action contributes to the idea that Spielberg is saying the murder is justified, but I don't agree. ﻿ ﻿I left the movie feeling very unsettled. There's a lot of emotional manipulation here, and a lot of scenes that ring very hollow thirty years later. And while this may be a strong technical achievement, as a film - as a work of art - I find it lacking.

This will be my longest review because it’s 1am and I’m pissed off that I can’t connect with Spielberg movies (Sorry Jon). I just don’t get it. It makes me irrationally frustrated that I can’t pinpoint why I don’t like Spielberg movies all that much. I’ve only ever loved two of his movies, Catch Me If You Can and Jaws. Literally all his other “masterpieces” including this one, I find to be just decent. He makes decent movies. The last 40 minutes or so of this movie, when the final battle begins, are good. I’m invested. The problem is, that’s 1/5 of this ridiculously long movie. Maybe the emotional beats would have hit for me if it wasn’t all relying on Tom Hanks, an actor I just don’t like. The technical movie making ability is obviously there, but they are all boring, even though the stories being told shouldn’t be boring. I mean, Indiana Jones , Jurassic Park , Saving Private Ryan . Three of his most beloved movies that I just didn’t care for all that much. Maybe they are just outdated and not made for modern audiences, but I don’t think that’s it. A thought just popped into my head. I dislike high sentimentality movies. Spielberg always makes these overly sentimental, borderline emotionally manipulative films to the point that it just pisses me off and takes me out of the movie. The score of this movie just feels so cheesy. It may be unfair to Spielberg as well, because I didn’t see any of these movies at the time they came out, and I’m sure they have influenced so many of these little tropes that I find annoying to watch now, but at the time they were inventive and new. Alright, enough ranting. This movie should have and easily could have been an hour shorter.
